references.text: The expression 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' is used several times by Jesus to describe the suffering of perdition. In Matthew 8:12, the same expression is used in a similar context where Jesus warns that the children of the kingdom will be cast out into outer darkness, while many will come from east and west and sit at the table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

The following verse, Luke 13:29, expands on the context by showing that people from all corners of the earth will sit at the table in God's kingdom, which reinforces the contrast with those who are cast out.
In Matthew 13:42, 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' is used regarding those thrown into the fiery furnace in the parable of the weeds, a parallel to the seriousness of judgment.
In Matthew 22:13, the expression is used in the parable of the wedding feast, where the one lacking wedding clothes is cast out into darkness—a parallel to being excluded from God's kingdom.
Matthew 24:51 uses the same expression regarding the unfaithful servant who is punished, emphasizing the seriousness of not being prepared.
In Matthew 25:30, the worthless servant is cast out into outer darkness with weeping and gnashing of teeth, another parallel to the warnings in Luke 13:28.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are mentioned as the patriarchs in God's kingdom. The promise to Abraham of blessing through his offspring is already found in Genesis 17:19, where God confirms His covenant through Isaac.
In Exodus 3:6, God reveals Himself as 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,' and Jesus uses this in Luke 20:37 as proof of the resurrection—the patriarchs live for God.

In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:23-26), the rich man sees Abraham far away with Lazarus at his side but cannot reach them—a dramatic illustration of seeing the patriarchs in God's kingdom while being excluded oneself.

Matthew 8:11-12 is the closest parallel to this verse: Jesus says that many will come from east and west and sit at the table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while the children of the kingdom are cast out into darkness with weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Psalm 112:10 speaks of the wicked who see it and are enraged, grinding their teeth and wasting away—an Old Testament background for the image of gnashing of teeth as an expression of despair and anger.
